import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 428

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/428](https://www.erdosproblems.com/428)
-/

open Nat Filter Set

namespace Erdos428

/--
The density ratio of set $A$ up to $n$ relative to the prime counting function $\pi(n)$.
-/
noncomputable def primeDensityRatio (A : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (A ∩ Icc 1 n).ncard / (primeCounting n)

/--
Is there a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, all of $n-a$
are prime for all $a\in A$ with $0 < a < n$ and $$\liminf\frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}>0?$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_428 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ A : Set ℕ,
      (∃ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ a ∈ A, 0 < a → a < n → (n - a).Prime) ∧
      liminf (fun n ↦ primeDensityRatio A n) atTop > 0 := by
  sorry

end Erdos428

reformulations.difference: The positive lower-limit condition uses an ℝ-valued Filter.liminf rather than an extended-real lower limit. Although primeDensityRatio can be unbounded for arbitrary A, this choice is equivalent under the theorem's prime condition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: At each qualifying n, the injection a ↦ n − a maps A ∩ [1,n] into {0} together with the primes ≤ n. Hence |A ∩ [1,n]| ≤ π(n) + 1, and for n ≥ 2 the ratio is at most 2. Qualifying n occur arbitrarily far out, while the ratio is always nonnegative. Its extended-real liminf is therefore finite, and positivity is equivalent to an eventual lower bound by some real c > 0. The real and extended-real versions of the full existential question were proved equivalent in /workspace/review/scratch.lean (Review428.full_question_iff), without using the sorry-backed problem theorem.

review.notes: Checked both declarations against the source. The source remains OPEN, matching the category and unknown yes-or-no answer. Lean checks confirm real rather than natural-number division, inclusive prime counting, finiteness of every counted intersection, and harmless zero-denominator values at n = 0,1. Also proved that finite A have density ratio tending to zero and that removing 0 from A changes neither condition. All scratch checks compile successfully; the equivalence proof depends only on standard Lean axioms.
